Admission is free to all visitors for three years starting January 2026, and the courtyard, multi-floor galleries, and historic stairwells reward an unhurried 90+ minute visit. Pair the museum with dinner at Casa Enrique (Michelin-starred Mexican, 8 min away) for a credible LIC museum→dinner track that justifies the drive from IC.
notes: Actually in Long Island City, Queens (not Williamsburg) — zone enum has no Queens option; tagged williamsburg as the closest Brooklyn proxy across Newtown Creek. Free admission for all visitors Jan 2026 through 2028 per institutional announcement (momaps1.org/visit). Weekend parking: Court Square Municipal Garage at 45-40 Ct Square W, ~6 min walk to the Jackson Ave entrance (nyctourism.com). Metered street parking on Jackson Ave is available but unreliable on Saturdays. Drive from Industry City via Hugh L. Carey Tunnel + FDR or BQE runs ~20-25 min on weekends. Headline 2026 show: 'Greater New York 2026' (Apr 16–Aug 17, 50th-anniversary survey of 50+ NYC-area artists) plus Red Canary Song's 'Touch the Heart' (Mar 19–Aug 17). Warm Up music series returns summer 2026 — schedule TBA on momaps1.org/calendar. Closed Tue/Wed; open Thu-Mon.

name: Donna (relocated to West Village)
desc: Worker-owned modern-tropical cocktail bar — original Williamsburg location closed 2020, now at 7 Cornelia St in the West Village
longDesc: Founded in 2012 in South Williamsburg by Leif Huckman, Donna closed in 2020 after a landlord sale and reopened May 2023 at 7 Cornelia Street as NYC's first worker-owned cooperative cocktail bar. The 'modern tropical' menu reflects its Cuban, Puerto Rican, Mexican, Venezuelan, Colombian, Salvadoran and Filipino worker-owners — signatures include the Tiny Sparrow Martini (Vietnamese gin, calamansi), the Umami Old Fashioned (shoyu, Charanda añejo, mushroom), Lolo Avo (rum, avocado, coconut), and the frozen Brancolada. Interior nods to Cuban Concretism and Brazilian Neo-Concretism — bold colour, dramatic shapes, dim romantic lighting.
notes: IMPORTANT — task premise is stale: the Williamsburg original at 27 Broadway closed in 2020 (Yelp/Resy confirm). Donna 2.0 is in the West Village (Manhattan), not Williamsburg — it no longer fills a Williamsburg slot. Owner attribution in the task ('Leandro Feal') does not match public record; the founder is Leif Huckman and the bar is now run by its worker-owners (Resy, Time Out, Spirits Business 2025-09). For a Saturfun trip anchored at Industry City this means: ~25-30 min drive via Battery Tunnel or Brooklyn Bridge, brutal weekend street parking in the West Village, and likely fails the 'driving + 10-25 min from IC' rule. Recommend NOT promoting to itinerary as the Williamsburg romantic-drinks slot — surface as a Manhattan-only special pick or replace with a true Williamsburg/Cobble Hill candidate (see enqueue). Cuban/Latin/Filipino program is genuinely strong if a Manhattan detour is justified (Casa Malka partnership announced 2025-09, Resy 2023, Time Out 2023).

name: The Long Island Bar
desc: Restored 1951 corner saloon turned modern-classic cocktail bar by Toby Cecchini, on Atlantic Ave.
longDesc: A diner-era corner bar from 1951, reopened in 2013 by Cosmopolitan creator Toby Cecchini and Joel Tompkins, now a fixture on World's 50 Best lists (#64 on North America's Best Bars in 2025). Mid-century neon, terrazzo floors, and a tight menu of precise classics (gimlets, daiquiris) and seasonal originals; bar food leans burgers and patty melts. Walk-in only — go right at the 2pm Saturday open, or stack it as the second move after dinner.
notes: Walk-in only, no reservations — biggest operational risk vs. Sunken Harbor Club (thelongislandbar.com). Corner of Atlantic Ave & Henry St; metered street parking on Atlantic and side streets, generally findable on weekends before 6pm. Closed Mondays; Tue-Fri 17:00-24:00 (yelp.com). Same Cecchini ownership as Sunken Harbor Club in Brooklyn Heights, so cocktail bar is exceptional — good defensive backup if SHC's walk-in line is long. ~12 min drive from IC via Hicks St / BQE.

name: Rainey Park (Astoria Waterfront)
desc: Free East River promenade on Vernon Blvd — direct skyline views, contiguous with Socrates Sculpture Park
longDesc: Reopened July 2025 after an $8.5M reconstruction, Rainey Park is a 7.6-acre waterfront strip in Astoria/LIC running along the East River with unobstructed views of Roosevelt Island and the Midtown Manhattan skyline. The new layout adds expanded greenways, a spray plaza, two-section playground, soccer field, basketball courts, picnic areas, and bike racks. Walk the promenade north and you flow straight into Socrates Sculpture Park, then Hallets Cove — a single Vernon Blvd parking session unlocks ~0.6 mi of continuous skyline walking.
notes: ACTUAL LOCATION: Vernon Blvd between 33rd Rd & 34th Ave, Astoria, Queens 11106 — not Brooklyn (zone enum forced to closest waterfront analog `dumbo`). Drive from Industry City via Gowanus/BQE ~25 min weekend, longer weekdays. Free street parking on Vernon Blvd; Socrates Sculpture Park's free lot (32-01 Vernon Blvd, ~2 min walk south) is the standard anchor — park once, walk the whole strip. Reopened 2025-07-09 after $8.5M NYC Parks reconstruction; pre-2025 photos show the old layout (source: qns.com 2025-07; nycdotprojects.info). Skyline views face west across the East River toward Roosevelt Island + Midtown — best light is late afternoon / golden hour. Sunset views especially strong June-September. Park officially closes 21:00; promenade walkway technically accessible later but unlit sections exist.

name: Astoria Park & Pool (Hell Gate Bridge views)
desc: NYC's largest/oldest free outdoor pool, riverside promenade framed by the Hell Gate and RFK bridges.
longDesc: Astoria Park anchors NW Queens with a 54,450 sq ft Olympic-trial-era pool (the city's biggest, free) plus the Shore Boulevard Promenade hugging the East River directly beneath the steel arch of the Hell Gate Bridge. Outside pool season (late June through early September) the park still delivers a running track, picnic lawns, and the most cinematic ground-level Hell Gate + RFK Triboro framing in the city. Pair with Socrates Sculpture Park and Bohemian Hall to make a full Queens day from Industry City.
notes: Free admission. Pool open ~late-June to early-September with a daily 3-4pm cleaning break (NYC Parks). NYC public-pool rules: plain white t-shirt over swimsuit required to enter deck, padlock required for locker, no phones/cameras in pool area. Weekend parking lot at park entrance on 19th St and a second lot under the RFK Bridge at Hoyt Ave N. Shore Boulevard Promenade is the photo spot — best light is golden hour for Hell Gate Bridge silhouettes. Drive from IC: BQE north to Triborough/RFK Bridge, ~30 min off-peak weekend.

name: The Bier and Cheese Collective (Ditmars)
desc: Curated craft-beer bottle shop + cheese counter — customize a 4-pour flight to pair with a cheese board.
longDesc: The surviving Astoria outpost of the former Astoria Bier & Cheese (the Broadway location closed in 2025), this Ditmars storefront keeps the same beer-and-cheese DNA: 12 rotating taps with build-your-own 4-beer flights, mix-and-match six-packs from 200+ bottles/cans, and a counter of cheeses and charcuterie cut to order. Pairing plates and meat-and-cheese boards make it a low-effort late-afternoon graze; staff are working cheesemongers and will guide flights if you ask. Adjacent to the Astoria–Ditmars N/W terminus on the 31st St corridor.
notes: IMPORTANT: the user-named location (Astoria Bier & Cheese, 34-14 Broadway) permanently closed in 2025 per Queens Post (https://queenspost.com/over-50-businesses-close-in-astoria-in-the-past-two-years-latest-being-selo-restaurant-on-broadway). This entry redirects to the operating sister bar at 35-11 Ditmars Blvd under the rebranded name 'The Bier and Cheese Collective' — same owners, same craft-beer-plus-cheese concept (bierandcheese.com). Located in Astoria, Queens (not Brooklyn — zone field set to nearest geographic enum value 'greenpoint' which borders Astoria across Newtown Creek). Drive from Industry City ~28-32 min via BQE — past the user's 10-25 min preferred radius, justified only as a third-stop add-on to a Greek-meal anchor in Astoria. Build-your-own 4-beer flight (12 taps), pairing plates pair four 5oz pours with labeled cheeses (~$18 at the prior Broadway shop; menu rotates with kegs). Weekend parking generally findable on side streets off Ditmars (29th-33rd Sts); Sundays suspend alternate-side rules. Vegetarian-friendly by default; vegan/GF require staff guidance on individual cheeses.

name: Prospect Park Audubon Center at the Boathouse
desc: Lakeside Beaux-Arts boathouse and free nature center on the Lullwater — turtles, warblers, ranger-led walks.
longDesc: The 1905 Beaux-Arts Boathouse sits on the Lullwater and houses the Audubon Center, the first urban nature center in the country. Weekends bring free animal encounters, naturalist-led nature walks, and birdwatching intros (Apr–Oct programming season). Pair it with a 20-minute loop walk to the Lullwater Bridge and Camperdown Elm — easy, low-cost third stop after BBG/Brooklyn Museum.
notes: Free admission and free public programming; closest entry is Lincoln Road / Ocean Ave (east side of park) — much closer than Grand Army Plaza if you're driving in from IC (Prospect Park Alliance). No on-site parking, but a ~30-car lot one block away and ample weekend street parking on Ocean Ave (SpotAngels). Programming resumed Apr 11, 2026; check the May 16 NYRR Brooklyn Half Marathon overlap which can affect park access on race morning. Building is the only lakeside structure left and a NYC Landmark — strong photo stop (Wikipedia).

name: Cheryl's Global Soul
desc: Globally-spiced brunch & comfort food a 5-min walk from Brooklyn Botanic Garden's east entrance.
longDesc: Chef Cheryl Smith's longtime Prospect Heights spot serves world-inspired soul food — buttermilk pancakes with Chantilly cream, salmon hash with poached egg, jerk wings, coconut-curry bowls, and a cranberry-blue salad for veg eaters. Brunch runs weekend mornings first-come-first-served (expect a wait 11am–1pm), so anchor here before walking down Eastern Parkway to BBG or the Brooklyn Museum.
notes: 236 Underhill Ave, ~5-min walk from BBG's Eastern Pkwy/Washington Ave entrance and the Brooklyn Museum (cherylsglobalsoul.com). Weekend brunch is first come first served starting 10am with peak waits 11am–1pm (yelp.com). Menu blends Southern soul with global flavors — pancakes w/ Chantilly + blueberry compote, chicken & pancakes, salmon hash, jerk wings, coconut curry wings bowl, tonkatsu bowl, plus veg salads (cherylsglobalsoul.com). Street parking on Underhill/Washington is realistic on weekends; lot at Brooklyn Museum is a backup. Phone (347) 529-2855.

name: Lefferts Historic House
desc: 1783 Dutch Colonial farmhouse in Prospect Park — free, photogenic 30-min curiosity stop
longDesc: A rare surviving Dutch Colonial farmhouse built c. 1783 by Peter Lefferts, moved into Prospect Park's Children's Corner in 1918 to save it from demolition. Reopens for the 2026 season Thursday May 14 with 'The Shirley Chisholm Way: Brooklyn's Blueprint for Change' (through Nov 15); weekends bring a working garden, indigenous-history exhibits, and hands-on demos like butter churning and flint-and-steel fire making. Admission is a $3 suggested donation, making it an easy, low-commitment add-on between BBG and Prospect Heights food stops.
hoursWeekend: Thu-Sun 12:00-17:00 (seasonal; Jul-Aug until 18:00; closed winter, reopens spring 2026)
notes: Located at Prospect Park's Children's Corner inside the Willink entrance (Ocean Ave + Flatbush Ave + Empire Blvd) — 5-min walk from Brooklyn Botanic Garden, so pairs naturally with a BBG/Crown Heights track (prospectpark.org). 2026 season opener May 14: Shirley Chisholm exhibit runs through Nov 15 (brooklyneagle.com). $3 suggested donation; jointly operated by Prospect Park Alliance + Historic House Trust (historichousetrust.org). No dedicated lot — use Empire Blvd or Ocean Ave street parking on weekends, or park near BBG and walk over.

name: New Leaf Restaurant & Bar
desc: Historic 1930s fieldstone cottage in Fort Tryon Park serving contemporary American — on-site to the Cloisters.
longDesc: Set inside a restored Olmsted-era stone cottage steps from The Met Cloisters, New Leaf serves casual-elegant contemporary American with a garden patio for weekend brunch. Proceeds from the restaurant support the New York Restoration Project, which maintains Fort Tryon Park. It's the only sit-down option inside the park itself, letting a Cloisters visit unfold without re-parking.
notes: Manhattan exception — paired with a Cloisters day trip rather than the IC 15-min cluster (forttryonparktrust.org). Free parking on-site and around Margaret Corbin Circle (forttryonparktrust.org/visit-and-park-map/getting-here). Drive from IC: Gowanus → Battery Tunnel → West Side Hwy → Henry Hudson Pkwy to exit 14/Fort Tryon, ~35-45 min off-peak. Reservations recommended for weekend brunch on the patio (opentable.com). Yelp shows a stale 'closed' tag — official site and OpenTable confirm active 2026 service.

name: Dyckman Farmhouse Museum
desc: 1784 Dutch Colonial farmhouse — last of its kind in Manhattan; $1 admission, Saturday only
longDesc: Built c. 1784 by William Dyckman, this is the only remaining Dutch Colonial farmhouse in Manhattan, sitting on a small green lot at Broadway and 204th in Inwood (dyckmanfarmhouse.org). The interior is furnished as a working-family farmhouse with hearth kitchen, parlor, bedrooms, and a reconstructed Hessian hut and smokehouse out back. At $1 admission and ~45 minutes to tour, it pairs naturally with The Cloisters as a short uptown-Manhattan history chain.
notes: Actually located in Inwood, Manhattan (4881 Broadway at 204th St) — chained stop, only justifies the drive when paired with The Cloisters ~10 min north in Fort Tryon Park. Admission $1 adults, free under 10; advance tickets recommended (dyckmanfarmhouse.org/tickets). No on-site parking — use street parking on Payson/Riverside Dr or the Fort Tryon Park lots and walk down (dyckmanfarmhouse.org). Closed Sun/Mon/Tue; only Saturday works for a weekend itinerary. Closed Juneteenth, July 4, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve/Day.

name: Hispanic Society Museum & Library
desc: Free Beaux-Arts museum with Goya, Velázquez, El Greco, and a Sorolla room in Washington Heights
longDesc: Tucked into the Audubon Terrace complex on Broadway at 155th, the Hispanic Society holds the largest collection of Spanish art outside Spain — Goya's Duchess of Alba, Velázquez portraits, El Greco, Luisa Roldán, and an entire vaulted gallery of Joaquín Sorolla's Vision of Spain murals. Admission is free; free street parking sits right alongside the building on 155th west of Broadway, and the Cloisters is a 6-minute drive further up Fort Washington Ave for a same-trip double-header.
notes: Free admission; starting Jan 2, 2026 reserve a free timed ticket online before visiting (hispanicsociety.org). Free parking on W 155th St west of Broadway adjacent to the building, one-way eastbound from Riverside Dr (hispanicsociety.org/visit/visitor-information/directions/). Kinney garage backup at 614 W 153rd St. Manhattan-only but uniquely justified: pairs naturally with the Cloisters (~6 min further north) on the same northbound drive. Sorolla's Vision of Spain gallery is the photo moment (newyorklatinculture.com).

name: Flushing Meadows Corona Park — Unisphere & Lake Loop
desc: Free 12-story stainless-steel globe from the '64 World's Fair plus a flat lake-loop walk — zero admission, big-sky photos.
longDesc: The Unisphere is a 140-foot, 120-foot-diameter stainless-steel globe built as the theme symbol of the 1964 New York World's Fair (motto: 'Peace Through Understanding') and now the centerpiece of Flushing Meadows Corona Park's main promenade. From there a flat promenade and the Meadow Lake loop give you 30-60 minutes of easy walking, big skyline sightlines, and unforced photo geometry — fountains around the globe are currently out of service (2025, electrical), so plan for the sculpture-and-sky composition rather than the spray. It pairs naturally with NYSCI (north) and Queens Botanical Garden (east) into a 3-stop Flushing day with one parking session.
notes: Actual location is Queens (Corona/Flushing), not Brooklyn — zone field uses 'industry-city' as a fallback only because the enum lacks Queens; treat as a Flushing-day anchor. Park itself: NYC Parks general hours 6am-1am; Unisphere plaza unfenced and walkable any time (nycgovparks.org). Globe = 140 ft tall, 120 ft diameter, built 1963-64 for the World's Fair (Wikipedia: Unisphere). Unisphere fountains AND mist garden have been out of service since 2025 due to electrical issues — don't promise spray (Wikipedia: Unisphere). Park is ~897 acres with Meadow + Willow Lakes south of the LIE; the Meadow Lake promenade is the natural loop walk (Wikipedia: Flushing Meadows–Corona Park). Heads up for drivers: Tide Gate Bridge on Meridian Rd inside the park is closed to vehicles, follow detour signage (nycgovparks.org). From Industry City: BQE → Gowanus → Grand Central Pkwy E, exit 9E Northern Blvd/Citi Field; ~14 mi, 25-30 min weekends. Closest paid lot is Citi Field / US Open Parking by the pedestrian bridge at 14 Ederle Promenade; Parking Lot A inside the park is the canonical Unisphere lot (parkopedia, spothero). Queens Museum sits at the west end of the same promenade — built into a 3-stop day it's a wet-weather backup that doesn't require moving the car.

name: Joe's Shanghai (Flushing) — PERMANENTLY CLOSED
desc: Original 1994 Flushing soup-dumpling shop; permanently closed — do not include in itineraries
longDesc: Joe's Shanghai opened its original Flushing location at 136-21 37th Ave in 1994 and was widely credited with introducing Shanghainese xiao long bao (crab-and-pork soup dumplings) to mainstream NYC diners. The Flushing storefront is now permanently closed per Yelp's April 2026 listing, Google's 'permanently closed' marker, and Foursquare; the brand continues to operate at 46 Bowery in Manhattan Chinatown and a Midtown location. Reddit threads reference a fire as a contributing factor, though the parent site joeshanghairestaurants.com still shows a stale Flushing page.
notes: DO NOT PROMOTE. Flushing original at 136-21 37th Ave is permanently shuttered as of confirmation April 2026 (Yelp listing tagged CLOSED, Google 'permanently closed', Foursquare 'Now Closed'). Original task brief assumed it was the iconic Flushing lunch-bridge between QBG and NYSCI — that assumption is stale. Zone is a placeholder; venue is in Flushing, Queens (not Brooklyn). Brand still operates at 46 Bowery (Manhattan Chinatown) and Midtown 49th St (Joe's Tower 49 spin-off). For the QBG/NYSCI lunch-bridge purpose, redirect to Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao or White Bear instead (queued).

name: Louis Armstrong House Museum
desc: Jazz legend's preserved Corona home — 40-min guided tours hourly, Thu-Sat only
longDesc: Satchmo's modest 1943 row house in Corona, Queens, preserved exactly as Louis and Lucille Armstrong left it — wallpapered den, mirrored bathroom, and his reel-to-reel tape collection. Visits are 40-minute guided tours capped at 10 people, departing hourly; a small exhibit and Japanese garden flank the house. Pairs naturally with Queens Botanical Garden or the Queens Museum for an eastern-Queens cultural day.
notes: Actually in Corona, Queens (not Brooklyn — routed under williamsburg as nearest gateway zone). Address: 34-56 107th St, Queens NY 11368. House Tour + Exhibit $20 adult / $14 senior-student-child; Exhibit-Only $10/$8 (louisarmstronghouse.org). Tours hourly on the hour, doors 10:45, final tour 15:00 — advance booking required, max 10 per tour. CLOSED Sunday-Wednesday — Saturday is the only weekend day this works. Street parking 'very limited' per the museum; weekend cleaning is not in effect but spots fill — allow 10 min to find a space or rideshare from the 7-train at 103 St-Corona Plaza. Drive from IC ~25 min via BQE → Grand Central Pkwy. New $26M Armstrong Center across the street opened 2023 with archives and a 75-seat performance venue.

name: NY State Pavilion — Tent of Tomorrow Tours
desc: Philip Johnson's 1964 World's Fair landmark, mid-restoration, with occasional guided interior tours
longDesc: The Tent of Tomorrow — a 350×250 ft elliptical ring of 100-foot columns originally roofed with multicolored fiberglass panels — is the surviving centerpiece of the 1964–65 World's Fair NY State Pavilion, designed by Philip Johnson. It's currently inside a $50M NYC Parks/EDC restoration slated through October 2026, with limited guided interior tours expected to resume late 2026; until then access is via Open House New York weekends, the Only in Queens Summer Festival, and Untapped New York's occasional guided walks. Pairs naturally with a Unisphere + Queens Museum stop in Flushing Meadows Corona Park.
hoursWeekend: Park dawn–1am; pavilion interior tours by event only
notes: Drive: BQE → Grand Central Pkwy, exit at Jewel Ave / Flushing Meadows; free lots near the Queens Museum and Unisphere fountain are closest to the pavilion. Exterior is viewable any time through the perimeter fence; interior access requires a scheduled tour — check OHNY (Open House New York) October weekends, the Only in Queens Summer Festival, and Untapped New York's tour calendar. Restoration scaffolding may obscure the south observation tower through Oct 2026 ($50M project, NYC Parks + EDC). Towers and tent perimeter are now illuminated every night post-2023 electrical upgrade (NYC Parks press release). The 567-tile terrazzo Texaco road map floor is the marquee feature once interior tours reopen.

name: The Lemon Ice King of Corona
desc: Since-1944 Italian ices stand with 30+ daily-made flavors, across from Spaghetti Park in Corona, Queens.
longDesc: A genuine NYC institution founded by Peter Benfaremo in 1944 and still hand-cranking real Italian ices from fresh fruit, with rotating flavors like lemon, peanut butter, cherry-vanilla, chocolate chip, and pistachio. Cash-friendly, takeaway-only, and best paired with a walk across the street to William F. Moore (Spaghetti) Park where the bocce courts run all weekend. Open 365 days a year.
notes: Actually located in Corona, Queens (52-02 108th St) — zone enum has no Queens slot, so 'industry-city' is a placeholder; add a 'corona' or 'queens' zone before promoting. Drive from Industry City via Gowanus/BQE/LIE is ~30 min on weekends, longer in summer (Tripadvisor, Infatuation). Parking is notoriously tight — locals double-park; consider street parking on 51st Ave or Roosevelt Ave. Cash strongly preferred. Hours vary by source and season (Yelp lists Mon-Fri 12-20 in shoulder season; summer extends to ~22:00). Pair with bocce in Spaghetti Park directly across the street (Epicenter NYC, NYC Tourism). Most ices are dairy- and gluten-free by recipe, but cream-based flavors (cherry-vanilla, chocolate chip vanilla base) are not vegan — ask before ordering.

name: Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao (K-Town)
desc: Manhattan K-Town outpost of Flushing's famed Lucky Six soup-dumpling house — closer-to-IC XLB fix.
longDesc: The Manhattan branch of the cult Flushing Shanghainese spot, opened July 2022 at 24 W 33rd St in Koreatown. The signature is the photogenic 'Lucky Six' tasting flight of color-coded xiao long bao (pork, crab & pork, chicken, scallop & pork, black truffle & pork, gourd luffa with shrimp & pork). Menu mirrors the original — wontons in peanut sauce, stuffed scallion pancakes, spicy beef & tripe, pan-fried pork buns — in a minimal wood-toned room with landscape art.
notes: MANHATTAN venue, not Brooklyn — 24 W 33rd St between 5th & 6th Ave, K-Town (Secret NYC). Same Lucky Six XLB as the Flushing original without the 35-45 min drive out to Queens. Route from IC: Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel → FDR/local streets, or BQE → Manhattan Bridge → straight up to 33rd. Parking: paid garages on W 32nd/33rd/34th (Icon, GMC) run ~$25-40 for 2-3 hr weekend; street parking effectively impossible. Walk-in friendly but expect 20-40 min weekend wait at peak — they take call-ahead. Vegetable dumplings and scallion pancakes cover vegetarians; everything else is meat/seafood. Phone (212) 970-3888.

name: White Bear
desc: Cash-only Flushing counter famed for #6: pork wontons in roasted chili oil
longDesc: A tiny, no-frills strip-mall counter on Roosevelt Ave whose Order #6 — twelve tender pork wontons bathed in a roasted-chili oil flecked with charred pepper bits — is widely cited as the best wonton plate in NYC. Cash only, ~$10, in-and-out in 20 minutes; pairs perfectly with Nan Xiang's soup dumplings ~5 min away on Prince St for a Queens single-dish crawl.
notes: ACTUAL LOCATION: 135-02 Roosevelt Ave, Flushing, NY 11354 (Queens — schema zone enum has no Flushing/Queens option, set to industry-city as placeholder; recommend adding 'flushing' to zone enum). Cash only — bring $20+ (Yelp, Food52). Closed Wednesdays — weekend OK (Yelp). Order #6 = 12 pork wontons in chili oil, ~$10 (Food52, TimeOut). Counter-service, ~6 seats, expect a short line on weekends. Pair with Nan Xiang Xiao Long Bao (~5 min walk, also in Flushing) for a two-stop Queens crawl. Drive from IC ~28-32 min via BQE+Grand Central Pkwy off-peak — outside the 10-25 IC radius but justified by the Nan Xiang pairing per task brief.

name: Tianjin Dumpling House (Golden Mall)
desc: Basement stall in Flushing's Golden Mall slinging lamb & green-squash dumplings, 12 for ~$6.
longDesc: A tiny counter on the lower level of the Golden Shopping Mall food court, famous for hand-folded lamb and green-squash dumplings — gingery ground lamb cut with light gourd, almost soup-dumpling juicy when boiled or pan-fried to a crackly crust. Beyond the signature, the menu fans out to sea bass and dill, fennel and pork, and a build-your-own-three-ingredient option. Cash-leaning, picture menus, eat at a shared bench in the food court.
notes: Stall-style counterpart to a sit-down Flushing dumpling stop — the trip-justifier here is the lamb + green-squash combo, a Tianjin specialty rarely done well outside of Flushing (The Infatuation; NYC Foodie). Inside Golden Shopping Mall basement at 41-28 Main St; mall itself runs ~9:00-21:30 (Yelp, May 2026). Cuisine-unique enough to anchor the long drive flagged in the task brief.

name: Xi'an Famous Foods — Tangram Flushing
desc: Hand-ripped biang biang noodles, liang pi, and spicy cumin lamb burgers in the Tangram food hall.
longDesc: The current flagship-sized Flushing location of Xi'an Famous Foods, replacing the original 500 sq ft Golden Mall stall with a 1,500 sq ft open-kitchen counter inside Tangram. Order the N1 spicy cumin lamb hand-ripped noodles, the liang pi cold-skin noodles, and a stewed pork or cumin lamb 'burger' on house flatbread — all the original family recipes, now with seating at long communal tables.
notes: Tangram Mall Level C, 133-33 39th Ave, Flushing NY 11354; open daily 11:00–20:30 (qns.com, yelp). The Golden Mall original at 133-31 is permanently closed (yelp). Tangram has a public parking garage on-site — best weekend parking option in Flushing. Walk from Flushing-Main St 7-train (~5 min) if not driving. N1 hand-ripped lamb noodle, liang pi, and cumin lamb burger all confirmed on the menu (xianfoods.com, clover).

name: New World Mall Food Court
desc: Basement food hall in Flushing with 28+ regional Chinese stalls — Lanzhou, mala, Uyghur, Pan Bao 66 soup dumplings
longDesc: The post-Golden-Mall pilgrimage for regional Chinese in NYC: a cavernous lower-level food court at 136-20 Roosevelt Avenue with hand-pulled Lanzhou noodles, two mala-tang/xiang-guo stalls (Lao Ma and Tian Fu Cuisine), Tarim Uyghur lamb-noodle and pilav, Pan Bao 66 soup-filled pork buns, Xian-style lamb pancakes, and bubble tea from Tiger Sugar and Gong Cha. Order at multiple counters cafeteria-style, sit at communal tables; dishes mostly $8–$14. Worth the cross-borough drive for the breadth — no Brooklyn analog exists at this density of regional specialists.
notes: Actually located in Flushing, Queens — outside the standard 15-min IC cluster but uniquely justified as the modern successor to Golden Mall's regional-Chinese vendor ecosystem (theinfatuation.com). On-site parking garage at the mall, accessible via BQE → Grand Central Pkwy. Official tenant list confirms Lan Zhou Handmade Noodles (#13), Lao Ma Ma La Tang (#14), Tian Fu Cuisine mala xiang guo (#21), Pan Bao 66 (#26), Tarim Uyghur Food (#4), Xian Noodles lamb pancake (#25), Joe's Steam Rice Roll (#3) (newworldmallnyc.com). Tarim Uyghur is halal; many vegetable/noodle stalls offer meat-free options. Note: 'flushing' or 'queens' zone may need to be added to corpus schema — tagged greenpoint as least-wrong placeholder.

name: Xi'an Famous Foods — Williamsburg (Hand-Ripped Biang Biang)
desc: Watch hand-ripped biang biang noodles slapped to order at Jason Wang's Williamsburg flagship
longDesc: Xi'an Famous Foods' open noodle station lets you watch cooks rip biang biang dough into wide ribbons before they hit boiling water — the same wrist-and-gravity technique CEO Jason Wang demos in his Bon Appétit test-kitchen video and 92Y cooking class, and documents in the 2020 Abrams cookbook (Xi'an Famous Foods: The Cuisine of Western China). Order the Spicy Cumin Lamb Hand-Ripped Noodles or the vegetarian Mt. Qi mushroom version; pair with Liang Pi Cold-Skin Noodles for a 30-minute counter meal that doubles as a kid-friendly noodle-theater stop.
notes: Address 209 N. 8th St., Brooklyn NY 11211 (xianfoods.com locations page). Counter-service, no reservations. Hand-ripping happens behind the counter — best viewing from the right side of the queue. Cookbook + 92Y class + Bon Appétit demo make this a strong lore-card anchor for cultural context (see TikTok @bonappetitmag/video/7231350616310730026). Street parking tight on weekends; nearest pay lots on Berry/N 7th or the McCarren-area garages. Vegetarian: Mt. Qi mushroom hand-ripped, Liang Pi cold-skin, tiger veggie salad.

name: Old Street Pan Fried Dumpling 老街生煎
desc: Cash-only Flushing counter for crispy-bottomed sheng jian bao with pork or crab+pork filling.
longDesc: Hole-in-the-wall snack shop on Roosevelt Ave a block from the 7 train and across from New World Mall, specializing in Shanghai-style pan-fried buns with thin crispy bases and a burst of hot soup. Order the classic pork or the crab-and-pork sheng jian bao, plus their spicy chicken or celery boiled dumplings and meat pancakes — most items run a few dollars and the line moves fast. Pairs naturally with a Flushing food-crawl day (New World Mall food court, White Bear wontons, Liu Liu Sheng Jian for a side-by-side bao comparison).
notes: Actually in Flushing, Queens (not Brooklyn — closest enum match used). 135-45 Roosevelt Ave, next door to New World Mall and steps from the 7 train terminus (oldstreetpanfrieddumpling.com). Cash-only, tiny counter, very limited seating — best as a takeaway stop on a Flushing dumpling crawl (ethnojunkie.com). Drive from Industry City via BQE+Whitestone or LIE runs 35-45 min on weekends; street parking around Roosevelt is brutal — use the Flushing Municipal Lot 1 (Lippmann Plaza) or the New World Mall garage. Phone 929-335-6666 (yelp.com).

name: Sky View Center (The Shops at Skyview)
desc: Flushing's parking-friendly mall anchor — 2,500 spaces, 3 hrs free, dessert + boba inside and next door
longDesc: Six-level garage at 40-24 College Point Blvd with 2,500 spaces and the first 3 hours free — the rational base camp for a Flushing food/dessert crawl by car. The mall itself houses BJ's, Target, Bowlero and a food court; the real prize is that New World Mall (Meet Fresh, food court, bubble tea) is a 4-minute walk south, so you park once and graze both buildings without hunting a meter on Main St.
notes: Actually in Flushing, Queens — using 'industry-city' as fallback until the zone enum gains 'flushing' (schema gap already queued). Parking garage open ~early morning to midnight, 3 hrs free with validation (theshopsatskyviewny.com/parking). Mall hours Sat-Sun 10-8; some restaurants and the garage stay open later. Pair with Meet Fresh at 133-36 37th Ave (New World Mall, Mon-Thu/Sun 12-9, Fri-Sat 12-10) for post-crawl black sugar boba shaved ice or Q-mochi milk bingsu. From IC: BQE → Grand Central Pkwy → Northern Blvd, ~25 min off-peak, 30-40 min Saturday lunch rush.

name: Gantry Plaza State Park
desc: Restored gantry cranes, Pepsi-Cola sign, and the most cinematic Midtown skyline view in Queens.
longDesc: A 12-acre LIC waterfront park built around the preserved Long Island Rail Road float-bridge gantries, with four piers that put you directly across the East River from the UN and Midtown. The restored neon Pepsi-Cola sign and the gantries themselves are a top-tier golden-hour photo backdrop, and the lawn + piers make it an easy chill stop before or after dinner in LIC. Free, open daily 8:00-22:00, with a small dedicated park parking lot at 46th Ave & Center Blvd plus several commercial garages within two blocks.
notes: SCHEMA GAP: this venue is in Long Island City, Queens, not Industry City. Zoned to 'industry-city' as the closest legal enum value pending the `long-island-city` addition flagged in this crawl's reason. Route from IC: BQE N -> Pulaski Bridge -> 11th St (~22 min off-peak, 30+ min Sat afternoon). Park lot at 46th Ave/Center Blvd fills fast on weekends; SpotHero garages on Center Blvd and 5th St are reliable backups (source: spothero.com). Free entry, no reservation, dogs on leash, restrooms on site (source: parks.ny.gov, nyctourism.com).

name: Carroll Park
desc: Shady Carroll Gardens square with benches and a playground — perfect bench-picnic stop for CSG sandwiches.
longDesc: One of Brooklyn's oldest neighborhood parks, Carroll Park sits at 375 Court St between President and Carroll, a 5-minute walk south of Court Street Grocers. The shaded bench area and tree-lined paths make it the natural picnic landing for sandwiches, with a playground, basketball, and bocce going on around you on weekends. It's a real neighborhood scene, not a tourist green — local families, dog walkers, and bagel-eating regulars (visitbrooklyn.nyc, onthegrid.city).
notes: Pair with a sandwich pickup at Court Street Grocers on Smith St (~5 min walk via Sackett or President). Street parking is realistic on weekends along Smith, President, or Carroll Sts; metered closer to Court. Benches in the shaded southwest corner are the picnic-friendliest. Restrooms onsite. Address: 375 Court St between President & Carroll (nycgovparks.org). Weekend energy is family/playground-heavy — bring shades and claim a bench early (onthegrid.city).

name: Caputo's Fine Foods
desc: Family-run Italian deli on Court St since 1973 — fresh mozzarella, cured meats, and house pasta
longDesc: A boutique Italian grocer in Carroll Gardens, family-owned and operated since 1973 when Giuseppe and Flora Caputo opened it after emigrating from Southern Italy. The Court St shop is beloved for its fresh-pulled mozzarella, house-made pastas and ravioli, imported cured meats, and a deep selection of olive oils, sauces, and Italian pantry staples. It's the older-school counterpart to nearby G. Esposito and Frankie's, a quintessential stop on a Court St food crawl.
notes: 460 Court St between 3rd and 4th Place; closed Mondays (caputosfinefoods.com). Closes early Sunday (2:30 PM) — best as a Saturday late-morning/midday stop. Pairs naturally with G. Esposito (pork store, half a block away) and Frankie's 457 (Court Street Spuntino) for a 'Court St food crawl' track. Weekend metered street parking on Court St; side streets (3rd/4th Place, Luquer) usually have spots on weekends.

name: A.I.R. Gallery
desc: Free DUMBO nonprofit gallery — longest-running all-women artists cooperative in the US, since 1972.
longDesc: A.I.R. (Artists in Residence) is a 50+ year old feminist artist cooperative on Plymouth Street, two blocks from the Brooklyn Bridge. Rotating exhibitions of women and non-binary artists fill a clean ground-floor space that's wheelchair accessible via ramp. Pairs naturally with Smack Mellon and Klompching for a DUMBO gallery walk.
notes: Free admission, wheelchair-accessible via ramp, accessible restrooms, complimentary tap water (airgallery.org/visit). Nearest accessible parking garage at 100 Jay St, two blocks away — relevant since surrounding cobblestone streets are rough. F train at York St is 0.2 mi if anyone subways in. Closed Mon-Tue, so this is a Wed-Sun stop only.

name: Time Out Market New York (Empire Stores Rooftop)
desc: 24,000 sq ft food hall in DUMBO's Empire Stores with a 5th-floor rooftop facing both bridges.
longDesc: Curated food hall inside the restored 1869 Empire Stores warehouse on the Brooklyn waterfront, packing ~20 vetted vendors (Bark Barbecue, Ess-a-Bagel, Fornino, Clinton St. Baking, Jacob's Pickles, Mori Mori) plus three bars across two floors. The fifth-floor rooftop has open sightlines to the Brooklyn Bridge, Manhattan Bridge and lower Manhattan skyline — the payoff stop after a DUMBO gallery loop. Order downstairs, carry up; arrive before sunset on weekends since the rooftop fills fast.
notes: Address: 55 Water St, Brooklyn NY 11201, inside Empire Stores (timeout.com). Rooftop is 5th floor with Brooklyn + Manhattan Bridge views (empirestoresdumbo.com). Parking is tight on-street but ~1,200 off-street spaces within two blocks (empirestoresdumbo.com/visit-us). Multi-vendor format covers most dietary needs incl. vegetarian, bagels, BBQ, pasta, dumplings; verify vegan/halal/GF at individual stalls. Best paired upstream with a 45-60 min gallery stop on Water/Front St before walking over.

name: Red Hook Boaters Free Kayaking
desc: All-volunteer free kayaking off Louis Valentino Pier, Sunday afternoons in summer.
longDesc: Since 2006, the Red Hook Boaters have run a completely free, first-come-first-serve kayaking program inside the protected cove at Louis Valentino Jr. Pier Park. They provide club kayaks, Coast Guard-approved PFDs, and a quick safety brief; paddles are capped at ~15-20 minutes per person so the line keeps moving. Sundays 1-4pm (June through late September) are the weekend slot; Thursdays 6-8pm run a shorter June-August window. Minors must paddle with a legal guardian present.
notes: Free, no reservations — line forms at the pier (redhookboaters.org/home). Sunday 1-4pm runs ~Jun 1 to late Sep; rides limited to 15-20 min each, so go early in the window for a shorter wait. Park on Coffey/Van Brunt — Red Hook has free street parking on weekends. Pair with Hometown BBQ, Pioneer Works, or a Brooklyn Crab drink afterward. Note: 2026 dates not yet posted as of May 2026; pattern matches 2025 schedule (redhookboaters.org/general-info).

name: The Four Horsemen
desc: Michelin-starred natural-wine bar with seasonal small plates, co-owned by LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy
longDesc: A Williamsburg natural-wine institution at 295 Grand St, co-owned by LCD Soundsystem frontman James Murphy and run by chef Nick Curtola. Holds a Michelin star (2019) and a James Beard Award for its wine list, with a daily-changing menu of small plates designed around the bottle list. Intimate, low-lit room — listening-bar-adjacent energy, made for slow weekend dinners.
notes: Fri-Sun 11:00am-10:45pm; Mon-Thu dinner only from 5:30pm (Yelp). Address 295 Grand St, Brooklyn NY 11211. Reservations via Resy strongly recommended — books out fast on weekends. Drive ~22 min from Industry City via BQE; street parking on Grand/Havemeyer is doable on weekend afternoons but tight after 6pm. Michelin star since 2019; James Beard Award for wine program (vinepair.com).

name: Eavesdrop
desc: Greenpoint audiophile listening bar with Danley speakers, natural wine, cocktails, and izakaya plates.
longDesc: A 1,000 sq ft jazz-kissa-inspired listening bar at 674 Manhattan Ave, Greenpoint, with 36 seats and a custom sound system built around Danley SH60 loudspeakers and Seaton Submersive subs, fed by Technics turntables, Pioneer CDJs, and a MasterSounds Radius rotary mixer. Designed by Danny Taylor of House Under Magic with a diffusion wall and acoustic paneling, it pairs craft cocktails and a globe-spanning natural wine list (Italian pet nats, Spanish whites, Chilean skin contact, Australian reds) with small plates in an intentionally low-volume, conversation-friendly room. Co-founded by Charlie Ballinger, Max Dowaliby, Dan Wissinger and Taylor; reservations via Resy.
notes: Audiophile rig: Danley SH60 + Seaton Submersive subs, MasterSounds Radius rotary mixer (insheepsclothinghifi.com). Room designed by Danny Taylor / House Under Magic with diffusion wall + acoustic panels (archpaper.com). Inspired by Tokyo jazz kissa but tuned for conversation rather than dancing (eavesdrop.nyc). Natural wine list spans Italian pet nats, Spanish whites, Chilean skin contact, Australian reds (insheepsclothinghifi.com). Weekend street parking in Greenpoint is achievable north of the McGuinness corridor; arrive before 6pm Sat for best odds. Resy reservations recommended; only 36 seats.

name: Hart's
desc: Intimate Mediterranean dinner spot on Franklin Ave with wood-fired seafood and natural wine.
longDesc: Hart's is a candle-lit, 40-seat neighborhood restaurant from the Roman's/Marlow team serving a tightly edited Mediterranean menu — clam toast, whole roast fish, lamb burger — paired with a natural-leaning wine list. Reservations on Resy go fast; bar seats are walk-in friendly. Cozy enough to feel like a real evening anchor, not just a stop.
notes: 506 Franklin Ave at Fulton; technically Bed-Stuy/Clinton Hill border. Mediterranean small plates + whole fish; book on Resy 2-4 weeks out, walk-ins at the bar. Street parking on Franklin/Hancock is doable on weekend nights (source: hartsbrooklyn.com, resy.com). Michelin Guide listed.

name: Leyenda (CLOSED)
desc: PERMANENTLY CLOSED March 29, 2025 — Ivy Mix / Julie Reiner pan-Latin cocktail bar that ran 10 yrs on Smith St
longDesc: Leyenda was a James Beard–nominated pan-Latin cocktail bar at 221 Smith St in Carroll Gardens, opened 2015 by Ivy Mix and Julie Reiner with a tequila/mezcal/rum/cachaça/pisco program and food by Sue Torres. It closed permanently after service Saturday March 29, 2025, just shy of its 10th anniversary; Mix cited a changing neighborhood, building issues, and post-pandemic industry costs. The leyendabk.com domain still serves stale hours — do not route guests here.
notes: Permanently closed end of March 2025 after ~10 yrs (Time Out, Spirits Business, PUNCH). Final 'Legends of Leyenda' takeover series ran the last weeks; Ivy Mix's last shift was March 19, 2025. Mix is now co-owner of Whoopsie Daisy wine bar in Crown Heights (opened 2024) — that is the live successor for any 'Ivy Mix nightcap' slot. Leyenda's .com still shows hours and is misleading — flag for any auto-import. Keep this record so the corpus does not re-research the same dead address.

name: The Four Horsemen
desc: Michelin-starred Williamsburg natural wine bar with 800+ bottle list and seasonal small plates.
longDesc: James Murphy's (LCD Soundsystem) Grand Street wine bar earned its first Michelin star in 2019 and a James Beard Award for its 800+ bottle low-intervention wine list. Chef Nick Curtola's seasonal small-plates menu changes constantly, and the intimate dining room is one of the city's defining natural-wine rooms. A strong quieter closer to balance an Insa karaoke night.
notes: 295 Grand St, Williamsburg. Reservations release 30 days out at 7am on Resy and go fast; walk-ins seated at the bar work best right at 5:30pm open (Resy). Michelin star since 2019 (Michelin Guide). Seasonal small plates + 800+ natural wines, James Beard wine list winner (VinePair). ~20 min drive from IC up the BQE; metered street parking in Williamsburg, variable on weekend nights. Vegetarian-friendly small plates available; menu changes frequently so dietary asks should be confirmed at booking.

name: Hunters Point South Park
desc: LIC waterfront park with cantilevered skyline overlook, tidal salt marsh, and kayak launch.
longDesc: Sprawling 11-acre waterfront park directly south of Gantry Plaza, with a 30-foot cantilevered platform jutting over the East River for sweeping Manhattan skyline views. Phase 2 added 1.5 acres of newly-established tidal salt marsh wetlands, a kayak launch on Newtown Creek, and Nobuho Nagasawa's 'Luminescence' moon-phase sculpture installation that glows at night. Pair it with Gantry Plaza as one extended LIC waterfront stop — same drive, same parking pool.
notes: Park is technically in Long Island City (Queens) — closest zone in the corpus enum is Greenpoint, just across Newtown Creek. Drive from Industry City via Gowanus/BQE is ~18-22 min on weekend mornings; same parking pool as Gantry Plaza (street parking on Center Blvd / 2nd St is usually findable on Sat/Sun mornings, with the paid Hunters Point South Parking Corp garage at 5-49 Borden Ave as backup). Phase 2 (opened 2018) added the cantilevered overlook + salt marsh wetlands (NYC Parks press release 21586). The southern kayak launch on Newtown Creek supports free seasonal community paddles run by HPP Conservancy. 'Luminescence' moon-dome installation is especially photogenic at dusk (Untapped New York). Pavilion has restrooms + seasonal concessions.

name: Domino Park
desc: 6-acre waterfront park on the old Sugar Refinery site with elevated walkway and unobstructed Manhattan skyline views.
longDesc: Built on the former Domino Sugar Refinery in South Williamsburg, this Two Trees-developed park stretches a quarter-mile along the East River with a 30-foot elevated walkway supported by 21 preserved refinery columns. The lawn, fog bridge, and bocce/volleyball courts sit directly across from a wide-open Manhattan skyline — best at golden hour. In-park food comes from Tacocina (Danny Meyer's taqueria), so you can shoot photos and eat without moving the car.
notes: Entrance at 15 River St (entries along Kent Ave at S5/S3/Grand). Free; park is open daily 6am-11pm (dominopark.com). Tacocina open Fri-Sat 11am-10pm, Sun 11am-9pm (dominopark.com). No on-site lot; nearest paid parking is 325 Kent Ave garage, otherwise street parking on Kent/Wythe (hellolittlehome.com, bklyndesigns.com). Elevated walkway above Tacocina is the prime skyline-photo spot — early morning or pre-sunset avoids weekend crowds. Strong swap for LIC Gantry when BQE northbound times spike.

name: Shelsky's of Brooklyn
desc: Family-run appetizing counter — hand-rolled bagels, lox boards, smoked fish, schmears.
longDesc: Peter Shelsky's Court Street appetizing shop is Brooklyn's answer to Russ & Daughters: hand-rolled, kettle-boiled bagels, a deep smoked-fish case (gravlax, pastrami salmon, sable, whitefish), bialys, and herring. There's a small counter for sit-down bagel sandwiches and lox boards, plus catering platters — about a 12-minute drive from Industry City, with street parking on Court and the side streets on weekends.
notes: Sit-down seats are limited — counter-forward, expect a short wait on weekend mornings (yelp.com). Lox boards and the smoked-fish bagel sandwiches are the signature order; ask about pastrami salmon and gravlax cuts. Street parking on Court St and on Atlantic-side blocks is workable on Saturdays. Sister bakery 'Shelsky's Brooklyn Bagels' at 453 4th Ave (South Slope) is a separate stop — different hours, more of a grab-and-go bagel counter (shelskys.com).

name: Mile End Delicatessen
desc: Counter-service Montreal-style smoked meat deli — hand-cut brisket on rye, since 2010.
longDesc: Mile End brought Montreal's pepper-and-coriander-cured, hand-sliced smoked meat tradition to Brooklyn in 2010 and remains the city's reference point for it. The Hoyt St flagship is a tight counter-and-communal-table room serving the signature smoked meat sandwich, poutine, latkes, and a Canadian-Jewish breakfast menu on weekends. Tiny footprint, brisk turnover — grab a stool, order at the counter, or take the sandwich to-go from the sidewalk window.
notes: Address 97 Hoyt St, Brooklyn NY 11217 (Boerum Hill/Cobble Hill seam). Phone (718) 852-7510. Reservations available on Resy but most seating is counter/communal walk-in; sidewalk takeout window relieves the queue (yelp.com, resy.com). Street parking on weekends is reportedly easier than weekdays (yelp.com). Signature: Montreal smoked meat sandwich on rye with mustard; weekend brunch adds smoked-meat hash and challah french toast. Pairs with [[russ-and-daughters]] as a deli double-feature — smoked meat vs smoked fish — without overlapping cuisine.

name: Little Island at Pier 55
desc: Free elevated park-on-stilts in the Hudson with 360° city/river views, gardens, and an amphitheater.
longDesc: Heatherwick-designed 2.4-acre floating park built atop 132 tulip-shaped concrete pots rising from the Hudson, with three hillside lookouts, winding garden paths, and The Amph (a 700-seat amphitheater). Free walk-in, no reservations needed; sunset views over the river and Lower Manhattan skyline are the headline shot. Pairs naturally with a High Line walk — entrance is a 5-minute stroll from the Gansevoort stairs (littleisland.org).
notes: Manhattan day-trip justified by pairing with High Line southern terminus — 5-min walk from Gansevoort St entrance (triptins.com). Entrances at W 13th & W 14th St off the West Side Highway. No on-site parking; nearest garage MPG Manhattan Parking at 450 W 17th St between 9th/10th Ave (NBC New York). Free admission; only ticketed events are Amph shows ($25-$65). Drop-off on 10th Ave. Best at golden hour for skyline + river shots.

name: Chelsea Market
desc: Indoor food hall + boutique shopping under the High Line; the rain-day Manhattan anchor
longDesc: A 100,000+ sq ft indoor food hall in the old Nabisco factory in Meatpacking, packed with stalls like Los Tacos No. 1, Lobster Place, Mokbar, Miznon, and Amy's Bread. Sits directly beneath the High Line so the day pivots indoor-outdoor without a re-park, making it the strongest rain-day fallback for an Industry City–anchored itinerary. Two paid lots flanking the W 15th St entrance handle weekend parking.
notes: Manhattan venue — uniquely justified as the rain-day pairing with the High Line directly above (source: chelseamarket.com/visit). Address 75 Ninth Ave, NY 10011. Two adjacent paid lots with W 15th St entrances; budget ~$30+/2hr on weekends (source: spotangels). Drive from IC is 15-25 min via Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel + West Side Hwy. Zone tagged 'dumbo' as the closest Brooklyn-side proxy since the schema has no Manhattan enum — UI should treat as Manhattan rain-day add-on, not a Brooklyn cluster stop.

name: Hudson Yards: Vessel + Edge
desc: Twin Manhattan landmarks at the High Line's north end — climb the Vessel, then float 100 floors up on Edge's glass deck.
longDesc: Hudson Yards stacks two photogenic icons within one block: Thomas Heatherwick's 150-ft honeycomb Vessel (reopened March 2026 after a multi-year safety closure) and Edge, the Western Hemisphere's highest outdoor sky deck at 1,131 ft with an angled glass floor. Pair them with a Chelsea-to-HY walk down the High Line for a single-parking-transaction Manhattan day. Indoor Edge experience is partly under renovation through May 2026, with a new immersive installation debuting June 2026.
notes: Manhattan exception justified — northern terminus of the High Line enables a Chelsea Market → High Line → Hudson Yards loop on one parking ticket (Hudson Yards Garage, ~$30 weekend flat). Vessel GA $10, flex $15; NYC residents free Thursdays (vesselnyc.com). Edge GA from $39, sunset slots higher; book 14+ days out for early-bird (edgenyc.com). Edge indoor space limited Apr-May 2026 (renovation), new immersive June 2026 (decks-nyc.com). Vessel reopened March 2026 with new safety mesh (timeout.com).

name: The Noguchi Museum
desc: Isamu Noguchi's serene indoor/garden sculpture museum in a converted Astoria photo-engraving plant.
longDesc: Founded by Isamu Noguchi in 1985 inside a former photo-engraving factory, the museum houses the world's most comprehensive collection of his stone, metal, wood, and clay sculptures across two floors plus an open-air sculpture garden. The hushed concrete galleries and bamboo-fringed courtyard make it the meditative indoor counterpart to Socrates Sculpture Park four blocks south on Vernon Blvd, letting a single track pair free outdoor art with ticketed indoor minimalism.
notes: 9-01 33rd Rd, Astoria — technically LIC/Astoria border, ~22 min from Industry City via BQE. $16 general admission; free on First Fridays of every month (extended to 8pm May-Sept) (noguchi.org). Street parking is metered but generally findable on weekends in this industrial pocket — easier than Manhattan museums. Pairs naturally with Socrates Sculpture Park (free, 4 blocks north) for an indoor+outdoor sculpture afternoon.

name: Felix Roasting Co. – Astor Place
desc: PERMANENTLY CLOSED (Mar 2026): former NoHo Felix outpost at 2 Astor Pl
longDesc: Felix Roasting Co.'s Astor Place café opened in 2022 at 2 Astor Pl in NoHo as a smaller, more pared-back counterpart to the floral-baroque NoMad flagship. It permanently closed on March 19, 2026 and is no longer listed on the brand's Visit Us page. For a Felix experience, use the SoHo (145 Greene St) or NoMad (450 Park Ave S) locations instead.
notes: PERMANENTLY CLOSED as of 2026-03-19 per Yelp listing title 'FELIX ROASTING - CLOSED' (yelp.com/biz/felix-roasting-new-york-7). Not present on the official Visit Us page (felixroastingco.com/pages/visit-us), which now lists only Midtown (280 Park Ave), NoMad (450 Park Ave S), SoHo (145 Greene St), West SoHo at Hotel Hugo (525 Greenwich St), and Aspen. Geographically in NoHo, Manhattan — zone tagged 'dumbo' as the nearest IC-to-Manhattan crossing cluster (via Manhattan Bridge / Hugh L. Carey Tunnel, ~25 min weekend drive). Drop from active itinerary rotation; retain entry as a do-not-suggest record so the planner doesn't re-add it.

name: Ulysses' Folk House
desc: Stone Street's anchor Irish pub — oysters, Guinness, and cobblestone outdoor seating in FiDi.
longDesc: Sprawling Irish pub from the Harry's Restaurant Group on Manhattan's only pedestrianized cobblestone block, with the patio spilling out onto Stone Street three seasons a year. Menu runs from raw-bar oysters and Lobster Mondays to weekend brunch and classic pub grub, paired with Guinness, whiskeys, and craft beer. Live music in the Music Room and late-night DJs several nights a week keep it pulling well past dinner.
notes: 58 Stone St, FiDi. Manhattan exception: Stone Street is a unique pedestrian-only cobblestone destination, not replicable in Brooklyn — justifies the cross-river trip as part of a FiDi walk cluster (Fraunces Tavern, Battery, Seaport). Drive: Brooklyn-Battery / Hugh L. Carey Tunnel from IC, ~12-15 min off-peak; weekend street parking easier south of Bowling Green (Whitehall/Broad/State) than mid-FiDi. Outdoor seating only in 3 seasons (Apr-Oct). Hours: Mon 4pm-4am, Tue-Sun 11am-4am (source: ulyssesnyc.com). Cash bar; reservations only for large groups via Harry's Restaurant Group (source: harrysrestaurantgroup.com).

name: Fraunces Tavern & Museum
desc: 1719 tavern + museum where Washington bid farewell to his officers — restaurant downstairs, four floors of Revolutionary history upstairs.
longDesc: The oldest standing structure in Manhattan and a National Historic Landmark at 54 Pearl St, two blocks south of Stone Street. The ground floor still operates as a tavern (Independence Bar, Whiskey Bar, Tallmadge Room) while the upper floors house the Fraunces Tavern Museum, including the reconstructed Long Room where Washington said goodbye to his Continental Army officers on Dec 4, 1783. Curious-track gold: pair a museum walk-through with a beer + shepherd's pie at the bar.
notes: Manhattan exception justified: oldest building in the borough + the Washington Farewell room — no Brooklyn equivalent. Drive: BQE → Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel (I-478) → exit at West St, ~15 min off-peak weekend. Street parking is brutal in FiDi; use the Pier 6 / Battery Underground garages (5-7 min walk). Stone Street pedestrian-only block is a 2-block stroll for a follow-up drink. Museum admission ~$10 adults (sons-of-the-revolution operated). Restaurant has vegetarian options but is meat/whiskey-forward.

name: Brooklyn Bridge Walk: FiDi → Dumbo
desc: 1.1-mi pedestrian-only promenade from City Hall to Dumbo with skyline + East River views.
longDesc: Start on the Manhattan side at Centre St & Park Row (just east of City Hall) and walk the elevated wooden promenade across the East River, exiting at the Washington St & Prospect St stairs that drop you directly into Dumbo at the Manhattan Bridge framing shot. Since the 2021 redesign moved cyclists onto a dedicated former vehicle lane below, the entire upper boardwalk is pedestrian-only — much calmer and easier for photos. Free, 24/7, and the perfect way to close a Manhattan loop before getting picked up at Old Fulton St or driving from Dumbo back to IC.
notes: Walk west-to-east: Manhattan entry at Centre St & Park Row, ~1.1 mi / ~30 min steady or ~60 min with photo stops (Free Tours by Foot). Pedestrian boardwalk is now bike-free since the 2021 lane reconfiguration — significantly less stressful than pre-2021 (Brooklyn Bridge Park). Exit options on the Brooklyn side: Washington St & Prospect St (the iconic Dumbo stairs, lands you under the Manhattan Bridge arch for the postcard shot) or the Tillary & Adams ramp if knees prefer no stairs. For the FiDi→Dumbo loop after Stone Street, walk 8 min north to the Manhattan ramp, cross, descend at Washington/Prospect, then drive home from Dumbo (~15 min to IC via BQE). Bring a layer — it gets windy mid-span even in summer.

name: The Four Horsemen
desc: Michelin-starred natural wine bar from James Murphy with seasonal small plates and 800+ bottle list
longDesc: Opened 2015 by LCD Soundsystem's James Murphy and partners, this glowing cedar-clad room at 295 Grand St pioneered Williamsburg's natural wine scene and later earned a Michelin star. Expect veal sweetbread skewers, oeuf mayonnaise with caviar, butter beans in parmesan broth, and fennel-pollen-butter house bread alongside a low-intervention list deep enough to spend an evening on. Intimate, candlelit, '80s samba on the speakers — pair with Lilia or Delmano for a Williamsburg evening crawl.
notes: 295 Grand St, Williamsburg. Michelin-starred natural wine bar co-owned by James Murphy of LCD Soundsystem (The Infatuation review). 800+ bottle low-intervention list, small plates menu. Reservations strongly recommended via Resy; walk-ins possible at the bar early. Street parking in Williamsburg is doable on weekends but tight — budget 10 extra min. Pairs well with Lilia (pasta) or Delmano (cocktails) for a wine-forward Williamsburg evening track.

name: Kent Ave Garage (25 Kent / 82 N 13th)
desc: Walkable, flat-rate weekend garage one block from Wythe Hotel and the North Williamsburg waterfront
longDesc: Indoor garage at 82 N 13th St (entrance on Kent Ave) that locks in flat weekend rates starting around $16 via SpotHero and serves as the most practical parking anchor for the Wythe / William Vale / Domino Park cluster. Wythe Hotel itself has no on-site parking and no in-house valet (only a loading zone at N 11th & Wythe), so this garage is the de-facto drop-point for the Williamsburg track. From here it's a 3-4 min walk to Wythe Hotel, Lemon's rooftop, Marlow & Sons, and the Domino Park waterfront.
notes: Wythe Hotel has no on-site parking or valet (wythehotel.com/accessibilty). Nearest alternatives: William Vale Hotel valet at 113 N 12th St (literally next door, starting ~$24/2hr) and Valet Garage at 34 N 7th St (cheapest entry ~$6/2hr, 7-min walk). For weekend day-trips, prebook Kent Ave Garage on SpotHero for ~$15-23 flat (spothero.com/destination/nyc/wythe-hotel-parking). Loading zone at N 11th & Wythe allows quick drop-offs before parking.

name: Sweetleaf Coffee Roasters — Greenpoint
desc: Roaster-direct Greenpoint cafe two blocks off the Pulaski Bridge landing with realistic weekend curbside parking.
longDesc: Sweetleaf's Greenpoint flagship on Freeman Street pairs an on-site roastery with a bar-style espresso program and their signature Rocket Fuel (maple-sweetened cold brew with chicory). The block is residential, slow, and two-way — by Greenpoint standards it has actual weekend street parking, and it sits one short turn off the Pulaski Bridge deck so a Greenpoint coffee detour adds maybe five minutes to the LIC→IC return path.
notes: 159 Freeman St, Brooklyn, NY 11222. Saturday–Sunday 8am–7pm (sweetleafcoffee.com). Yelp + Greenpointers confirm ample street parking on Freeman/West/Java vs the impossible Manhattan Ave corridor (yelp.com, greenpointers.com). Roastery is on-site — opened Aug 2015 with the cafe in front (sprudge.com). Order the Rocket Fuel; it ties back to the LIC origin location at the other end of the Pulaski. From here back to IC is ~20 min via McGuinness → BQE west.

name: Baolala
desc: Industry City soup-dumpling counter — pork, crab, chicken, and spicy XLB, no Manhattan needed
longDesc: A quick-service Shanghainese spot tucked inside Industry City at 253 36th St, occupying the same address Yaso Tangbao made famous for soup dumplings. Baolala turns out xiaolongbao in pork ($9), crab meat, chicken, and spicy varieties, plus the namesake Bao La La soup noodle and rice bowls — solid casual stop that gets you the XLB fix on-site without crossing into Chinatown.
notes: Same 253 36th St address that Yaso Tangbao occupied through 2024; Baolala is the current operator and explicitly markets xiaolongbao as the signature (source: baolalany.com menu). Yelp confirms Tue-Sun 11-8 weekend window. For a Brooklyn-only itinerary this eliminates the Joe's Shanghai Chinatown drive — XLB is literally on the IC campus. Pork XLB is $9/order; crab meat variant is the upgrade pick. No reservations, walk-in counter format.

name: Chrystie Garage (MTP Parking)
desc: Chinatown commercial parking garage on Chrystie at Grand — the practical weekend park for Joe's Shanghai and Bowery dumplings
longDesc: Run by MTP Operating Corp at 89-93 Chrystie St (between Grand & Hester), this is the closest reliable garage to Joe's Shanghai (46 Bowery, ~2 min walk) and the Chinatown food corridor. Weekend rates in this micro-zone typically run $27-$35 for a daytime stay per SpotHero's Chinatown destination page; MTP's posted in-and-out is around $18 for 3 hours (non-SUV), which covers a lunch/dinner stop. Pull-in hours are Mon-Fri 6am-10pm, Sat-Sun 8am-7pm — note the earlier weekend close, so plan an evening pickup before 7pm or use a 24-hour alternative.
notes: Manhattan exception, justified: this is the lynchpin for any IC-to-Chinatown food run because legal weekend curb parking on Chrystie/Bowery is near-impossible (source: parkopedia Chinatown). MTP Chrystie posts ~$18/3hr non-SUV (source: yelp listing summary); SpotHero's Chinatown range cites $27-$35 weekend daytime — book ahead on SpotHero to lock the lower end. CRITICAL: Sat/Sun pickup window ends 7pm — dinner stops past 7pm need a 24hr alt (Chrystie has metered street and other garages, but this one closes early). Phone (212) 431-7778. Drive route: BQE → Manhattan Bridge → exit at Canal/Chrystie, ~22 min off-peak from IC.

name: Nom Wah Tea Parlor
desc: NYC's oldest dim sum parlor (est. 1920) on the bend of Doyers Street, Chinatown.
longDesc: Opened in 1920 as a bakery and tea parlor, Nom Wah is Manhattan Chinatown's longest continuously running restaurant, tucked into the elbow of historic Doyers Street. The Hong Kong-style dim sum is served à la carte (not cart) all day — the OG egg roll, soup dumplings, and roast pork bao are the canonical orders. Weekend lines form by noon; Resy reservations are the only reliable workaround.
notes: Manhattan exception justified: only viable if Chinatown leg pairs Nom Wah with a second nearby stop (Apotheke, Joe's Shanghai, MOCA, or Columbus Park) to amortize the bridge crossing. From IC: Gowanus Expy → BQE → Manhattan Bridge → exit Canal St, ~22 min off-peak, 30+ min midday Saturday. Street parking on Pell/Mott is non-viable on weekends — use Mahayana Buddhist Temple garage at 133 Canal St or SP+ at 75 Mulberry. Walk-ins wait 45-90 min on Sat/Sun; book Resy 14 days out. Cash and card accepted, ~$25-35/pp. Hong Kong-style à la carte ordering (sources: nomwah.com, yelp.com, wikipedia).

name: Hauser & Wirth Wooster Street
desc: Free blue-chip gallery in SoHo's Cast Iron District — 4,000 sq ft single-story space with 16.5-ft ceilings.
longDesc: Hauser & Wirth's third NYC location opened in fall 2023 at 134 Wooster Street, just north of Prince, in a 1920s former truck garage that's one of the few single-story buildings left in the SoHo-Historic Cast Iron District. The ground-floor gallery has 4,000 sq ft of column-free exhibition space under 16.5-ft ceilings, with rotating museum-grade shows (Roni Horn, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Allison Katz). Free admission, no booking — a strong SoHo anchor for itineraries skipping Tribeca.
notes: 134 Wooster St, just north of Prince — formerly a Gagosian space, then a 1920 truck garage (artnews.com, gothamtogo.com). Tue–Sat 10–18:00, closed Sun/Mon — so this only works for Saturday itineraries (hauserwirth.com). Free, no advance booking, wheelchair-accessible. Drive from IC ~18-22 min via Hugh L. Carey Tunnel; SoHo street parking is brutal on Saturdays — use a garage (SP+ at 100 Mercer or LAZ on Broome). Pairs well with The Drawing Center, Lehmann Maupin Chrystie, and Dover Street Market for a SoHo gallery loop.
